chunks: How are ICs made?. The question: How are ICs made?
An integrated circuit is built on a thin disc of pure silicon, layer by layer.
The same loop repeats many times: add a thin film, pattern it using light, then etch away material or shoot in atoms (implant), then clean.
The first layers make transistors, and later layers add copper wiring. Then the wafer is tested, cut into dies, and the good dies go into packages.
Think of silk-screen printing a poster with many colors. Each color goes on through its own stencil, and every stencil must line up exactly with the ones before.
Chips work the same way, with dozens of stencils.
One difference matters: a chip loop also removes material, by etching, and it changes the silicon's electrical properties, not just its color.
The main stages. Everything from FEOL to wafer probe happens on the whole wafer at once, in parallel. Only after probing is the wafer cut into individual dies.
Wafer: the pure silicon disc the chips are built on. Mask: a plate with a pattern, used like a stencil. Photoresist: a light-sensitive coating.
Light through the mask changes it, so some areas can be washed away. Etch: removing material only where the resist does not protect it.
Doping: adding a few atoms of another element to change how well silicon conducts.
Here is one trip around the loop. Grow a thin layer of glass (silicon dioxide) on the wafer. Dry oxygen at 1000 degrees Celsius for an hour grows about 69 nm.
Coat it with photoresist. Shine light through a mask, then develop it in a chemical bath, so resist remains only where you want to keep glass. Etch away the unprotected glass.
Strip the leftover resist and clean. You now have glass in exactly the pattern you drew.
A modern chip needs this loop dozens of times, up to about a hundred, and every layer must align with the last. All the dies on a wafer are built at the same time.
That is the whole idea.
"ICs are built on a pure single-crystal silicon wafer by repeating a loop: deposit a film, pattern it with photolithography, etch or implant, and clean and polish.
The front end builds transistors, and the back end adds copper wiring layers. Then you probe-test each die, dice the wafer, package the good dies and test again.
It's done in a cleanroom because one particle can kill a die."
